1.pericope_label: Speak the things which become sound doctrine: the aged men

schools.summary: Set the charge against the Cretan situation before glossing a word of it. Titus' first work had been organisation; his second and equally weighty mission was the refutation of a school of professed Christian teachers who were fatally lowering the tone of Christian life by their example, and it is that moral influence rather than the doctrinal error to which his attention is especially directed — which is why the charges are so remarkably practical, a quiet and useful life pressed on every age and rank before doctrine is touched. Note that the phrase for sound doctrine is peculiar to the Pastoral Epistles and stands against the sickly and fanciful teaching of the misleaders. On the aged men, rest the identification on the word: an unusual noun occurring nowhere else in the New Testament except twice, once in a gospel and once of Paul the aged, and in no instance applied to an office. Then take sobriety in a more extended sense than the bare literal meaning would give, the elder men thoughtful in contrast with the thoughtlessness of careless youth; and observe that patience here takes the place of hope in the familiar Pauline three, because enduring fortitude especially becomes the old man waiting for death, whose infirmities and loss of the friends of early years will soon be over — a few more sighs, and they will sigh no more.

Take the metaphor in earnest, since the adjective is doing the work. Doctrine is called sound from the effect produced by it: it means wholesome, that which actually feeds souls, and so serves not only for nourishment but for medicine, since we are full of vices which are worse than diseases. Press the comparison to an uncomfortable end — when we want food for the body we are immediately terrified and have not a moment of repose, because it touches us nearly, while we are insensible to all that affects our souls. Then divide sound doctrine into two parts, the one magnifying the grace of God in Christ so that we learn where to seek salvation, the other framing the life to the fear of God; and note that these things are to be spoken not once or twice but so long as the pastor holds his office.

Read the command as a conclusion drawn from the chapter before it. The Judaizing teachers not only taught a false doctrine but led an unholy life, and Titus was to act directly opposite, proclaiming a sacred doctrine and the things which become it, so that principle and practice go hand in hand. On the aged men, hold that the whole context requires the literal sense and that no office is in view; and keep sobriety concrete, since for an old man to be a drunkard and a trifler is not only blamable but monstrous — Seneca having said it already, that a young man addicted to luxury transgresses while an old man thus addicted runs mad.

Keep the charge on the man himself before applying it to anyone else: ordaining others to preach would not excuse Titus from preaching, nor might he take care of ministers and elders only, and ministers must not stay in generals but divide to every one his portion, which is why what follows is an excellent Christian directory accommodated to each age and condition. Report that some understand the aged men of elders by office, including deacons, before taking it of the aged in point of years; and ask of them that the inner man be renewed as the outer decays, since those who are full of years should be full of grace and goodness.

Explain why such an exhortation is needed at all, since age has failings that youth has not — a slowness, a timidity, a forgetfulness, an insensibility, an irritability — and many things at this period make men otherwise than vigilant, especially that general insensibility and the difficulty of stirring them. Note that among the old some rave and are beside themselves, some from wine and some from sorrow, for old age makes them narrowminded; and that patience is well added last, since this quality more especially befits old men.

debates.question: What does the word rendered 'sober' require of the aged men?

sides.position: Its literal force, abstinence and vigilance: for an old man to be a drunkard and a trifler is monstrous
A more extended sense than the bare literal meaning would give: thoughtfulness, in contrast with the thoughtlessness of careless youth

debates.question: Are 'the aged men' officers of the church?

sides.position: No: the noun is not the usual word for an elder, is never applied to an office, and the context requires plain old age
Some understand elders by office, including deacons; but it is rather to be taken of the aged in point of years

outliers.note: Alone develops the medical metaphor into an argument, that doctrine is called sound because it feeds and heals souls, and that our alarm when the body wants food beside our insensibility to what the soul wants is proof of how sensual and earthly we are; and alone divides sound doctrine into two parts, the magnifying of grace and the framing of life.

Alone catalogues the failings peculiar to age — slowness, timidity, forgetfulness, insensibility, irritability — as the reason vigilance must be enjoined, and alone observes that some of the old rave from sorrow as others do from wine.
Alone accounts for the substitution in the Pauline triad, patience standing where hope usually stands because enduring fortitude especially becomes the old man waiting for death.

themes: But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.

3.pericope_label: The aged women as teachers of good, and the young women

schools.summary: Set the charge in the larger frame first: Paul is faithful here to what had become one of the guiding principles of Christianity, the equal position of women as fellow-heirs in the city which hath foundations, and the position Christ and his disciples had claimed for them was not without grave responsibilities. Show that the word for demeanour covers dress, appearance, conversation and manner alike, an outward deportment dependent on something more internal, such as the younger and more thoughtless sister could respect and reverence as an ideal she might hope one day to reach; and gloss the compound rendered teachers of good things as found nowhere else, a sorely needed mission. Explain why the work is left to the women and not to Titus: such a reformation in individual life would never be brought about by a sermon or by many sermons however eloquent, but would follow from patient individual effort and holy example. Diagnose the Cretan disease as a feverish longing for excitement and novelty, women as well as men preferring the tithing of mint and anise and cummin to quietly doing their Father's business, and read Paul's correction as a recall to the steady performance of the quiet every-day duties to which God had called them. On the domestic charge, note that the older authorities read workers at home, that the sense is little changed, and that keeping at home never meant never going abroad, only that a wife not be better known abroad than at home; and add that no wealth or splendour, no magnificence of entertainment or sweetness of music, can compensate for the want of mutual affection, which will diffuse comfort through the obscurest cottage of poverty.

Deny that these are persons in office — neither ancient widows with some care of the poor nor presbyteresses, as some call them, but godly women in years, who are to be instructed and exhorted like the rest. On what they are to teach the younger, keep it practical: to be chaste, modest and temperate, and wise and prudent in their conduct toward their husbands and in the management of family affairs, having had a large experience of these things before them.

Believe elderly women are meant and not deaconesses, and let the dress, gait and general deportment be what the holy calling requires, decent without and adorned with holiness within. On wine, show how ordinary the reputation was: both among the Greeks and Romans old women were reputed fond of much wine, the ancient scholiast on Homer saying that at this age they delight in it and Ovid seeming to translate the words literally, so that the participle here means not merely given to wine but enslaved by it, habit being a species of slavery. Then press the connection into the next verse with Jerome's question, how an elderly woman can teach young women chastity when, if the young woman should imitate the drunkenness of the matron, it would be impossible for her to be chaste. On the household charge, prefer the reading of the older copies, workers at home rather than keepers at home, since a woman may keep the house very closely and yet do little in it for the support or comfort of the family; and supply the taunt the enemy will make — behold your boasted religion, our heathenism is as good as your Christianity.

Pair the virtues rather than listing them, since the pairing is the argument: discreet and chaste stand well together, because many expose themselves to fatal temptations by what at first might be but indiscretion; and chaste and keepers at home are well joined too, since Dinah lost her chastity when she went to see the daughters of the land. Allow that occasions for going abroad exist and will exist, and name the real evil as a gadding temper for merriment and company's sake, to the neglect of domestic affairs; then add the sharper thought, that those whose home is their prison may be feared to find their chastity their fetters. Take good in both senses, generally in opposition to all vice and particularly of one kind and helpful, of a meek and yet cheerful spirit, not sullen nor bitter, not of a troublesome or jarring disposition uneasy in herself and to those about her.

debates.question: Should the household word be read 'keepers at home' or 'workers at home'?

sides.position: Workers at home, with the older copies and versions: a woman may keep the house very closely and yet do little in it for her family
The older authorities do read workers at home, but the sense of the passage is little changed by the alteration
Keepers at home, without notice of the variant: characteristically attentive to their domestic concerns

debates.question: Are 'the aged women' holders of an office?

sides.position: Not only those who may hold the office of deaconess, but all aged females
Elderly women are meant and not deaconesses; not ancient widows, nor presbyteresses as some call them

outliers.note: Alone assembles classical evidence that old women were reputed fond of wine, citing the ancient scholiast on Homer and what looks like a literal translation of the same words in Ovid; and alone brings Jerome's question to bear, that a matron's drunkenness makes it impossible for the young woman who imitates her to be chaste.

Alone explains why this teaching was committed to the women rather than to Titus, on the ground that a reformation of individual life is not brought about by sermons however eloquent but by patient individual effort; and alone diagnoses the Cretan disease as a feverish longing for excitement which preferred the tithing of mint and anise and cummin to quietly doing the Father's business.

Alone reaches for Dinah going to see the daughters of the land as the warning behind pairing chaste with keepers at home, and alone turns the charge back on itself with the observation that those whose home is their prison may be feared to find their chastity their fetters.

themes: The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.

6.pericope_label: The young men, and Titus himself a pattern of good works

schools.summary: One word is all the young men get, so explain why it is enough. Take it as a well-governed mind, superior to the indulgence of those passions to which the young are prone, and give the reasons the charge is pressed on them in particular: the hopes of the church depend much on them, a young man who cannot govern himself gives little promise of being useful or happy, indulgence sooner or later brings ruin to body and soul alike, they stand at the period of life most exposed to peculiar temptations, and they may soon die and should be habitually ready to stand before God. Explain also why the task falls to Titus, who in respect of age must still be reckoned among them — brought up in a Pagan home, not improbably in luxurious and wicked Syrian Antioch, drawn to the Master's side in the fresh dawn of manhood and tried in many a difficult task, he was about forty when placed over the Cretan Church. On the pattern, hold that neither uncorruptness nor gravity refers to the subject-matter of the teaching but to the bearing of the teacher, who must be above seeking popular applause and must keep his gravity in private intercourse with his flock and not only in the delivery of sermons; note that sincerity is wanting in the older copies and name the editors who reject it, and that uncorruptness is the only example of its word in the New Testament. Take sound in its ordinary medical sense of healthful or whole, and observe that in this figurative use it belongs in the New Testament to Paul alone. On the closing clause, agree that the older authorities read of us rather than of you, and draw the consequence, that what might have been said against Titus would in reality be spoken against Paul and the elder Apostles.

Put the order of reformation the other way about: it should begin with the old, who have the authority and should give the example, though the young of both sexes must also give account of themselves to God, and sober-mindedness in young men is a rare qualification, for want of which they plunge into excesses that sap the foundation of the constitution and bring on premature old age. Refer the words we translate in all things not to conduct generally but to the classes just named, so that Titus is to be a pattern to each of them, being in sobriety and gravity and temperance what he requires others to be; and read uncorruptness in doctrine as mixing nothing with the truth, taking nothing from it, adding nothing to it. On sound speech, press the figure: human nature is in a state of disease, all false doctrines leave men under its influence, and the unadulterated doctrine of the Gospel alone can heal them. Report that a large body of copies and versions read of us rather than of you, and call that reading undoubtedly genuine.

Name the besetting sin of the young exactly — there are more young people ruined by pride than by any other sin — and ask of them the seriousness of age joined with the liveliness and vigour of youth, which will make even those younger years pass to good purpose and yield matter of comfortable reflection when the evil days come. On the charge to Titus himself, state the principle underneath: preachers of good works must be patterns of them also, since without this he would pull down with one hand what he built with the other, and a defect here is both a great blemish and a great hindrance. Then say what the preaching must not be: the display of wit or parts, or of human learning or oratory, is not to be affected, and it must appear that the design is purely to advance the honour of God and the welfare of souls, the office being entered on with no secular view, neither from ambition nor from covetousness.

debates.question: What do the words 'in all things' belong to?

sides.position: Not conduct generally but the classes just named: Titus is to be a pattern to old and young, men and women, and servants alike
The pattern in its widest sense: a ceaseless activity prescribed to the superintending presbyter, in quiet days as in times of danger
It is possible to take them with 'sober-minded' in the preceding verse, though the editors take them with what follows

debates.question: Does the last clause read 'no evil thing to say of you' or 'of us'?

sides.position: Of us, on a large body of copies and versions; the reading is undoubtedly genuine and makes the better sense
Of you, without notice of the variant

outliers.note: Alone reconstructs Titus' own history to explain why the young men were his charge — a Pagan upbringing, not improbably in luxurious and wicked Syrian Antioch, conversion in the fresh dawn of manhood, and an age of about forty when he was set over the Cretan Church — and alone quotes Chrysostom that no task is so hard for youth as mastery over oneself in the matter of harmful pleasures.

Alone numbers the reasons sober-mindedness is pressed on the young in particular, ending on the one least often made, that they may soon die and should live as in the immediate presence of their Maker and Judge; and alone names the editors who reject 'sincerity' from the text.

Alone extends the medical figure from the doctrine to the patient, holding that human nature is in a state of disease which all false doctrine leaves untouched and only the unadulterated Gospel can heal.

themes: Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.
In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity,
Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you.

9.pericope_label: Servants adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour

schools.summary: Say plainly that these words are addressed to slaves, since the accurate translation is bond servants and the class is massed here under one head; and suspect the charge was called out by particular instances of insubordination and impatience among the Cretan slaves. State frankly what the difficulty was — that Christianity had the hard task of persuading the bondman, fellow-heir of heaven with the freeman, that the Master who promised him a home among the many mansions did not mean the existing framework of society to be changed at once. Render the phrase for answering again as not gainsaying, and give the tone: obedience without sullenness, not thwarting or setting themselves against their masters' plans. On purloining, supply the opportunity rather than the reputation, since many slaves in the empire were employed beyond house and farm, some entrusted with shops and left quite to themselves, others elaborately trained and working as artists or even physicians, so that a slave had a hundred ways of showing true fidelity as against assumed surface obedience. Then let the ornament be the point: Paul is showing slaves how they may adorn the teaching of God, and it is noteworthy how God deigns to receive an adornment from those ranked as possessions, just like cattle or horses. Turn it upward at the last — a master should feel the obligation not to be surpassed in religious character by his servant.

Bound the obedience before commending it: all their lawful commands ought to be obeyed, and in all things that are not contrary to a good conscience, to the Christian religion, and to the laws of God and nature. Then offer a second rendering of the clause about pleasing which the others do not entertain — that they may be well pleased in all things, that is, satisfied and contented with such things as they have and with their state and condition as servants, cheerfully abiding in the calling wherein they are called. On purloining, take the word in its exact sense of embezzling and keeping back part of what is committed to trust, as it is used in the case of Ananias and Sapphira.

Do not soften what these people were: the apostle refers to those who were slaves and the property of their masters, exhorted to obey their own despots though those had no right over them on the ground of natural justice, and required to please them in all things though they could not hope to succeed in every thing. On purloining, show how ordinary the vice was thought by assembling the Latin usage in which the word for a thief simply meant a servant: the line in Virgil's third eclogue asking what masters may do when servants dare such things, the note of Servius that the word for thief stands for a servant because thefts are peculiarly theirs, the taunt in Plautus that a man is one of three letters, and Terence's phrase for a company of servants as a bundle of thieves. It was necessary, therefore, that the apostle should be so particular in his directions to servants.

Give the duty its motive first: servants must know and do their duty to their earthly masters with reference to their heavenly one, since in serving an earthly master according to Christ's will Christ himself is served, and such shall be rewarded by him. Forbid disrespectful or provoking language, and require that a check or reproof be taken with silence rather than met with confident or bold replies; then add the reflex of guilt, that when conscious of a fault, to excuse or justify it doubles it. On fidelity, ask not only that nothing of the master's be put to their own use or wasted, but that his goods be improved and his thriving promoted; and close where the text does, that true religion is an honour to the professors of it and they should adorn it in all things.

debates.question: Does the charge address slaves in particular or servants of any condition?

sides.position: Slaves: the accurate translation is bond servants, and they were the property of their masters, who had no right over them on the ground of natural justice
Everything said here would be equally appropriate whether the servitude was voluntary or involuntary; a free man who takes service contracts to obey, not to reason

outliers.note: Alone documents how ordinary the vice was thought to be, collecting the Latin usage in which the word for a thief stood for a servant — the line in Virgil, the note of Servius upon it, the taunt in Plautus that a man is one of three letters, and Terence's bundle of thieves.

Alone offers a second rendering of the clause about pleasing which reverses its subject, so that the slaves are the ones well pleased — contented with their state and condition and cheerfully abiding in the calling wherein they are called.

Alone supplies the social detail that makes the temptation intelligible, that many slaves were entrusted with shops and left quite to themselves or trained as artists and physicians; and alone quotes Calvin's remark that God deigns to take an adornment from those ranked as possessions, just like cattle or horses.

themes: Exhort servants to be obedient unto their own masters, and to please them well in all things; not answering again;
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.

11.pericope_label: The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared

schools.summary: Report both constructions of the verse and prefer the marginal one as most in accordance with the Greek, holding the sense not essentially varied either way, since the plan was fitted for man as man and might include servants as well as masters, the poor as well as the rich. Render the whole as grace appearing and bringing salvation to all men, comparing the prophets on the light that is come and the Sun of righteousness arising with healing in his wings, and note that the verb for appeared is used in two other passages closely connected with Paul for the shining of the sun. Then guard the phrase, calling it one of those hard sayings pressed into the service of a kindly but erring school of expositors who shut their eyes to the warnings addressed to the impenitent: grace alone brings salvation to all men, which asserts not that all will be saved but that it is the only means by which salvation is possible. Take the participle for teaching as disciplining and educating us by life's sad experiences, God's grace being in truth a stern discipline of self-denial and training for higher things; read the three adverbs as one scheme of duty, to ourselves and our neighbour and our God; and carry the last phrase forward, since the present course of things is a transitory scene and the first manifestation in humiliation is an ever-present reminder to live in expectation of the second in glory.

Refuse the two easier readings before giving your own. It is not the free love and favour of God which lies in his own heart, for that has never been made manifest unto all men but is peculiar to the Lord's own people; nor is it the grace of God wrought in the hearts of believers, for that too has not appeared to all men, since all men have not faith nor hope nor love nor any other grace of the Spirit. It is the doctrine of grace, the Gospel of the grace of God, so called because it is a declaration of the grace of God and of salvation by it. Restrict the pupils in the same way: the 'us' who are taught are not all to whom the Gospel comes in its outward ministry, since many externally receive it and profess it who are never influentially taught by it, having a form of godliness but denying its power; the taught are those to whom it came not in word only but in power.

Build the whole comment on the figure the verb supplies, which is taken from the sun. As light and heat are denied to no nation nor individual, so from the influences of this spiritual Sun no soul is reprobated any more than from the natural one, only those being deprived who wilfully shut their eyes and hide themselves in darkness. That whole nations have not yet received the light is no objection, since the earth comes into the solar light successively, by its daily turning and by its passage through all the signs of the zodiac, and only when its year is completed has every part its due proportion; and men are not in total darkness before the Gospel reaches them, light having been created and dispersed three whole days before the sun was formed. On the teaching, open it to all who do not reject it, and take sobriety in the scripture sense to be rather the whole temper of a man than a single virtue in him, comprehending all that is opposite to the drowsiness of sin, the folly of ignorance and the unholiness of disorderly passions.

Make the link general rather than particular: let young and old, men and women, masters and servants and Titus himself all do their respective duties, for this is the very aim and business of Christianity, and grace is obliging and constraining to goodness, without which effect it is received in vain. Then press that the appearing is a matter of degree and of reach at once — the old dispensation was comparatively dark and shadowy, this a clear and shining light, and not to the Jews only, as the glory appeared at mount Sinai out of the view of all others, since the pale is now broken down and the doctrine is for all ranks and conditions, slaves and servants as well as masters. Take the teaching not as information and instruction only, as a schoolmaster does his scholars, but by way of precept and command, as a sovereign who gives laws to his subjects; for the gospel is not for speculation but for practice and the right ordering of life.

Read the conjunction backwards into the slaves' charge, since it is the ground of what precedes. Having demanded from servants so great a virtue as adorning the doctrine in all things, Paul adds the just cause why servants should be such: those who have God for their Teacher may well be so, seeing their numberless sins have been forgiven them, and nothing so awes and humbles the soul as to have had innumerable sins to answer for and to have received not punishment but pardon and infinite favours.

debates.question: In what sense has the grace of God appeared to all men?

sides.position: It is the doctrine of grace that has appeared, since neither God's favour in his own heart nor the grace wrought in believers has ever appeared to all men
Grace alone brings salvation to all men — which asserts not that all will be saved, but that it is the only means by which salvation is possible
As the sun's light is denied to no nation, no soul is reprobated from these influences; the unenlightened parts of the earth are coming into the light successively
Either construction will bear; the sense is not essentially varied, the plan being fitted to man as man

debates.question: Who are the 'us' whom the grace of God teaches?

sides.position: Only those taught with efficacy, not all who externally receive and profess the Gospel and are never influentially taught by it
All who do not reject it

outliers.note: Alone builds an extended astronomical analogy for the progress of the Gospel, arguing from the earth's daily turning and its annual passage through the signs that the nations come into the light successively, and from the creation of light three days before the sun that men were not in total darkness before the Gospel reached them.

Alone sets out the two-fold epiphany that governs the whole passage — the manifestation of the grace of God, which is past, and the manifestation of his glory, which is to come — and makes the first an ever-present reminder to live in expectation of the second.
Alone reads the verse as the ground of the charge to slaves rather than as a fresh beginning, finding the reason they can be asked so much in the pardon they have already received.

themes: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;

13.pericope_label: Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing

schools.summary: Render the clause as one object, the blessed hope and manifestation of the glory, and bind the two together, since the hope is the hope of glory we shall share with the Son when we behold him as he is. Note that the participle is the one used of those who were looking for the Messiah, and that the noun for manifestation means here the second epiphany where elsewhere it means the first. On the great God, say there can be little doubt the apostle meant the Lord Jesus, since the coming of God as such is nowhere taught and the phrase is applied in the New Testament to no other; if Paul did not mean this he used language fitted to lead men into error. List the names by which the reading has been vindicated; grant that on grammatical principles either translation would be possible, then pile up what is not balanced — the word for manifestation is used by Paul five times and always of Christ, never of the Father, and an epiphany of the Father would be an idea strange to the New Testament and dropped as soon as suggested. Make the weightiest argument the consensus of the Greek fathers, and add that one article governing both nouns gives the necessary meaning. On the last verse, do not let a peculiar people mean unlike others, however true that may be otherwise: the term means belonging to Christ rather than to ourselves, his own as a man's property is his own, and the passage should not be used to prove a distinctive manner of living. Elsewhere the contrast is the whole point, the phrase coming from the Greek Old Testament and from the people Jehovah would have peculiarly his own, set apart from a mankind lawless and idolatrous.

Work through the candidates for the blessed hope and reject the first: it is not the grace of hope, for that is already implanted in the heart at regeneration and cannot be said to be looked for. Allow that Christ himself, the object and ground of hope, may be meant, since he is our hope and Christ in us is the hope of glory; but because he is expressly mentioned in the next clause, prefer the thing hoped for — eternal glory and happiness, called elsewhere the hope of righteousness and the hope laid up in heaven, which will lie in the beatific vision of God and Christ, in perfect knowledge of them and communion with them, and in freedom from all evil outward and inward. On the next verse, hold that he gave not another nor another's but himself, all that was near and dear, his name and fame and credit, his time and strength and service, and the whole manhood as in union with his divine person, given into the hands of justice and to death itself as a ransom price.

Refuse to collapse the two objects into one. Some think the blessed hope and the glorious appearing mean the same thing, but they do not: the hope refers simply to eternal glorification in general, the appearing to the resurrection of the body, since when Christ appears he will change this vile body and make it like unto his glorious body. On the great God, translate the clause as the appearing of the glory of the great God, even our Saviour Jesus Christ, and send the reader to an essay on the Greek article for the structure and the doctrine together. Then read the last verse as a manumission: he gave his own life as a ransom price, and the word for a peculiar people signifies such property as a man has in what he has purchased with his own money, so that having bought the slaves from their thraldom he strips them of their sordid vestments and cleanses them, bringing them out of a servitude in which they had no motive to diligence and no affection for the despot over them, that they may become willing servants.

Expound the passage by the two comings, and let the prophets do the dividing. Malachi says the Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to his temple, and behold, that is the one coming; and again of the second, behold, he cometh, saith the Lord Almighty — but who shall abide the day of his coming, or who shall stand when he appeareth, because he cometh like a refiner's fire and like fullers' herb, and he shall sit as a refiner and purifier. Then note that the Saviour himself says immediately after, I will draw near to you in judgment and will be a swift witness; and that for this cause Paul warns us beforehand about what a man builds upon the foundation.

debates.question: Are 'that blessed hope' and 'the glorious appearing' one thing or two?

sides.position: Two: the hope is eternal glorification in general, the appearing is the resurrection of the body
One object: the blessed hope and manifestation of the glory, the hope being bound up with the second coming
Not the grace of hope, which is already implanted and cannot be looked for, but the thing hoped for — the eternal glory laid up in heaven
Ownership, not distinctiveness: they belong to Christ as a man's property is his own, and the passage should not be used to prove an unlike manner of living
The contrast is the whole point: a people peculiarly his own, set apart as Israel was from a mankind lawless and idolatrous
Such property as a man has in what he has purchased with his own money — slaves bought out of thraldom and made willing servants

outliers.note: Alone numbers his arguments that the great God is Christ, resting them on what the New Testament does not say as much as on what it does, and alone names the roll of scholars by whose labours the reading has been vindicated, including one who wrote on the Greek article.

Alone rests the case on the consensus of the Greek fathers as the weightiest argument available, quoting Theodoret that Paul here calls Christ the great God and so rebukes the blasphemy which denies his Godhead, and Chrysostom's question, what those can say who allege the Son is inferior to the Father.

Alone reduces the whole controversy to a point of syntax, that one article governing both nouns gives the necessary meaning, and notes that the participle for looking is the one used of those who awaited the Messiah.

themes: Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.

15.pericope_label: Speak, exhort and rebuke with all authority

schools.summary: Take the noun rendered authority to mean command, so that Titus was to speak decidedly, without ambiguity and without compromise and without keeping anything back, stating these things not as advice or counsel but as the requirement of God. Set the verse as the close of a division of the letter, a new division beginning with the chapter following, and hear in it the voice of the brave-hearted old man telling his disciple to speak with decision and to rebuke, if need be, with vigour, remembering the dark character of the people with whom he had to do — with the anxious warning in the background, that he show all diligence in his own words and doings so that every word of his may have its full weight. On the last clause, find the point in the verb, which is not the stronger word of scorn used elsewhere but one meaning to think around on all sides, so that the prohibition is literally that no man think around thee, the possibility being of someone making mental circles about a minister and so out-thinking him; from which draw the plain conclusion, that the best way to command respect for one's authority is to do thinking that will deserve it.

Gloss the three verbs in turn: the first means teach, and one manuscript actually reads the ordinary word for teaching; the second is to repeat them again and again and urge them on the attention and conscience; the third is to demonstrate their importance and necessity and show that God requires obedience. Take authority as that with which the office invests him and which he has received from God, and the last clause as a charge to act so that no person shall have cause to despise him, either for his work or for the manner and spirit in which he performs it. Then stand back from the whole chapter, since few portions of the New Testament excel it: it may well form the creed and system of ethics and text book of every Christian preacher, setting out what he is to believe, what to practise and what to preach, and even parcelling out his congregation to him, the old and young of both sexes and those in their employment. Draw four things from it in order — the duty of a Gospel minister, the Godhead of Christ stated so explicitly that the expressions cannot be misapplied, the extent of redemption with none passed by and none left without the first offer of life eternal, and the operation of grace in cleansing and purifying the soul for glory — and then turn on the reader, since neglect in such a case is the highest contempt which man can offer to his Maker.

Divide the verse into matter and manner. The matter is these things, not Jewish fables and traditions but the truths and duties just set out, so that ministers in preaching must keep close to the word of God and not the figments and inventions of their own brain. The manner is doctrine and exhortation and reproof together, and the exhortation is to be pressed with much earnestness, since ministers must not be cold and lifeless in delivering heavenly doctrine as if it were indifferent or of little concern, but must urge it with an earnestness suitable to its importance. On the last clause, say that the most effectual way for ministers to secure themselves from contempt is to keep close to the doctrine of Christ and imitate his example, to preach and live well and do their duty with prudence and courage; and add that he who despiseth despiseth not man but God. Then suggest a second addressee which no one else entertains — that an admonition might here be intended for the people, that Titus, though young and but a substitute of the apostle, should not be condemned by them but respected and supported in his work and office.

debates.question: Whom does 'Let no man despise thee' address?

sides.position: Titus alone: act so that no person shall have cause to despise thee, either for thy work or for the spirit in which thou performest it
Titus, and perhaps the people too, who should not condemn him for being young and but a substitute of the apostle, but respect and support him

outliers.note: Alone closes with a verdict on the chapter as a whole, that few portions of the New Testament excel it and that it may serve as the creed, system of ethics and text book of every Christian preacher, then numbers four doctrines drawn from it and turns on the reader with the warning that neglect here is the highest contempt a man can offer his Maker.

Alone rests the last clause on the choice of verb, which is not the stronger word of scorn used in the companion epistle but one meaning to think around on all sides, so that the danger is of being out-thought rather than merely looked down upon.

Alone reads the last clause as possibly addressed to the congregation as well as to Titus, so that the verse becomes a charge on the people to esteem and support a young minister rather than only a charge on him to deserve it.

themes: These things speak, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no man despise thee.
